claim: The Drosophila hindgut pylorus is the only segment of the hindgut to persist throughout the lifespan of the fly.
source: The pyloric epithelium is the only segment of the hindgut to persist throughout the lifespan of the fly.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text.

claim: Larval pyloric cells undergo mitotic cycles during metamorphosis to expand the larval pylorus into its adult form and produce cells of the adult ileum.
source: During metamorphosis, pyloric cells act as facultative progenitor cells, as they remodel the hindgut by undergoing mitotic cell division to both expand the larval pylorus into its adult form while also producing cells of the adult ileum, which replace the histolysed larval ileum (Figure 1A, Fox and Spradling, 2009; Robertson, 1936; Sawyer et al., 2017; Takashima et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Pyloric cells are capable of distinct cell cycles: mitotic cycles during organ remodeling at metamorphosis and endocycles during tissue injury repair in adulthood.
source: Thus, pyloric cells are capable of distinct cell cycles- mitotic cycles during organ remodeling (at metamorphosis) and endocycles during tissue injury repair (at adulthood).
evidence: Summary statement based on observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Injury to larval pyloric cells at the L3 stage results in adult pyloric cells that remain diploid with no change in cell ploidy.
source: When compared against uninjured animals (Figure 1C–C'), adult pyloric cells recovered from a larval injury (Figure 1D–D') show no change in cell ploidy and remain diploid (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 1G and images in Figure 1C-D'.

claim: Larval injury does not change the number or size of cells recovered in adults.
source: Additionally, larval injury does not change the number or size of cells recovered in adults (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–F',H).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 1H and supplementary figure data.

claim: Injury to adult pyloric cells persistently increases ploidy, decreases cell number, and increases cell size.
source: In contrast, comparable injury to the adult pylorus persistently increases ploidy, decreases cell number, and increases cell size, as we previously reported (Figure 1E,G,H, Losick et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1E, G, H and citation to previous work.

claim: Regardless of the severity of adult injury, cell number does not recover, whereas cell ploidy and cell size increases.
source: Regardless of the severity of adult injury, cell number does not recover, whereas cell ploidy and cell size increases (Figure 1F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1F, G and supplementary figures.

claim: Developmental stage and not injury severity dictates the pyloric cell cycle response.
source: Thus, developmental stage and not injury severity dictates the pyloric cell cycle response.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments varying injury severity.

claim: Ploidy increases closely track with the degree of cell number loss in adult pyloric cells after injury (R2 = 0.97, p<0.002).
source: Our quantitation of adult pyloric ploidy after injury revealed a proportional tissue injury response- ploidy increases closely track with the degree of cell number loss (Figure 1G–H, R2 = 0.97, p<0.002).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Regardless of injury severity or developmental stage, the pre-injury pyloric total genome content is fully recoverable.
source: Our data show that regardless of injury severity or developmental stage, the pre-injury pyloric total genome content is fully recoverable (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 1I.

claim: Through developmentally distinct cell cycle injury responses, the pylorus accurately restores genomic content in proportion to the injury stimulus.
source: These results indicate that through developmentally distinct cell cycle injury responses, the pylorus accurately restores genomic content in proportion to the injury stimulus (Figure 1J).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genome content quantification data.

claim: Single larval pyloric cells produce, on average, either ~5 adult pyloric cells or two adult ileal cells during metamorphosis, and afterwards cease to divide.
source: We previously used a low-background, low-frequency clonal marking system to demonstrate that single larval pyloric cells produce, on average, either ~5 adult pyloric cells or two adult ileal cells during metamorphosis, and afterwards cease to divide (Fox and Spradling, 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: In adults recovered from larval injury, clone size increases by ~3 fold on average compared to uninjured animals (uninjured: 5.389 ± 0.5725 SEM, injured: 16.54 ± 1.863 SEM, p<0.0001).
source: By comparison, in adults recovered from larval injury, clone size increases by ~3 fold on average (Figure 2D–D', G,H, uninjured: 5.389 ± 0.5725 SEM, injured: 16.54 ± 1.863 SEM, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2G, H with statistical analysis.

claim: Approximately 75% of larval cells were eliminated using the injury protocol and were then recovered by compensatory proliferation.
source: Our clonal data coupled with our cell counts suggest that approximately 75% of larval cells were eliminated using our injury protocol and were then recovered by compensatory proliferation.
evidence: Inference from clonal data and cell counts.

claim: Remaining larval pyloric cells (approximately 25%) have the capability of increasing their mitotic capacity to completely regenerate the adult hindgut pylorus and ileum following acute injury.
source: Further, these data show that remaining larval pyloric cells (approximately 25%) have the capability of increasing their mitotic capacity to completely regenerate the adult hindgut pylorus and ileum following acute injury.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from clonal analysis and cell count data.

claim: Inducing clones in adult pylori produces only single labeled cells (27/27 clones).
source: In contrast to larvae, inducing clones in adult pylori (Figure 2B) produces only single labeled cells (27/27 clones, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data in Figure 2E.

claim: No expansion of single labeled cells into mitotic clones was observed even after 20–30 days of recovery from a severe injury in adult pylori (uninjured: 1.00 ± 0 SEM, injured: 1.07 ± 0.07 SEM, p=0.99).
source: Using this system, we did not see any expansion of single labeled cells into mitotic clones even after 20–30 days of recovery from a severe injury (Figure 2F–H, uninjured: 1.00 ± 0 SEM, injured: 1.07 ± 0.07 SEM, p=0.99 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2F-H and supplementary data.

claim: The M-phase marker Phospho-Histone H3 (PH3) does not label adult pyloric cells.
source: In further support of our lineage data, the M-phase marker Phospho-Histone H3 (PH3) does not label adult pyloric cells (data not shown, Fox and Spradling, 2009; Sawyer et al., 2017), while it frequently labels larval pyloric cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and supplementary figure data.

claim: Both larvae and adult pyloric cells incorporate the S-phase marker EdU following injury.
source: However, both larvae and adult pyloric cells incorporate the S-phase marker EdU following injury (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J,K).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data in supplementary figures.

claim: Only larval pyloric cells divide while adult pyloric cells instead endocycle after injury.
source: Taken together, our cell cycle marker, lineage, and cell ploidy/number quantitation show that only larval pyloric cells divide while adult pyloric cells instead endocycle after injury.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including cell cycle markers, lineage tracing, and ploidy quantification.

claim: In the pylorus of uninjured larvae, the FUCCI components E2F11-230-GFP and Cyclin B1-266-mRFP are expressed in patterns consistent with the presence of G1, S, and G2/M cells.
source: In the pylorus of uninjured larvae, the FUCCI components E2F11-230-GFP and Cyclin B1-266-mRFP are expressed in patterns consistent with the presence of G1, S, and G2/M cells (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Supported by FUCCI reporter expression data in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Both before and after injury, larval pyloric cells undergo mitotic cycles, although injury leads to additional rounds of mitotic cycles.
source: Coupled with our M phase data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), we find that both before and after injury, larval pyloric cells undergo mitotic cycles, although injury leads to additional rounds of mitotic cycles (Figure 2L).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FUCCI and M-phase marker data.

claim: 100% of uninjured adult pyloric cells are E2F11-230-GFP positive and Cyclin B1-266-mRFP negative, indicative of a quiescent/arrested G0/G1 state.
source: In contrast, 100% of uninjured adult pyloric cells are E2F11-230-GFP positive and Cyclin B1-266-mRFP negative (Figure 2K), indicative of a quiescent/arrested G0/G1 state of these cells prior to their entry into injury-activated endocycles.
evidence: Supported by FUCCI reporter expression data in Figure 2K.

claim: Pyloric injury at distinct developmental stages induces distinct cell cycle changes.
source: Thus, pyloric injury at distinct developmental stages induces distinct cell cycle changes (Figure 2L).
evidence: Summary conclusion from FUCCI and cell cycle marker data.

claim: DEMISE combines the Gal4/Gal80ts and FLP/FRT systems to induce developmentally-timed, tunable tissue-specific injury in a mosaic fashion while independently expressing any UAS-driven transgene of interest in the same tissue.
source: We thus developed such a system, which we term DEMISE (Dual-Expression-Method-for-Induced-Site-specific-Eradication). DEMISE combines the Gal4/Gal80ts and FLP/FRT systems to induce developmentally-timed, tunable tissue-specific injury in a mosaic fashion while independently expressing any UAS-driven transgene of interest in the same tissue.
evidence: Description of the DEMISE method developed in this study.

claim: DEMISE adds an FRT-Stop-FRT cassette between a UAS promoter and the apoptotic rpr gene.
source: Compared to our previous injury system, DEMISE adds an FRT-Stop-FRT cassette between a UAS promoter and the apoptotic rpr gene (Figure 3A).
evidence: Description of the DEMISE construct design.

claim: In DEMISE, cell death and transgene expression are under control of a tissue-specific Gal4 and temperature inactivation of Gal80ts, but cell death also requires FLP-mediated removal of the Stop cassette.
source: Thus, cell death and transgene expression are still under control of a tissue-specific Gal4 and temperature inactivation of Gal80ts (Figure 3A') but cell death also requires FLP-mediated removal of the Stop cassette.
evidence: Description of DEMISE mechanism.

claim: Using DEMISE, all cells of a given tissue can express a transgene while a fraction of these cells (determined by degree of FLP induction) will be eliminated by injury.
source: The result is that all cells of a given tissue can express a transgene (such as a gene knockdown RNAi), while a fraction of these cells (determined by degree of FLP induction) will be eliminated by injury (Figure 3A''').
evidence: Description of DEMISE functionality.

claim: Using DEMISE in larval wing imaginal discs, transgene expression is induced in the expected pattern without inducing cell death.
source: Using temperature shifts and a UAS-GFP reporter, transgene expression is induced in the expected pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C). Our transgene expression conditions do not induce cell death, as assayed by TUNEL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary Figure 3-1A-C.

claim: Upon heat shock to induce FLP expression in DEMISE, robust cell death occurs in a mosaic pattern specifically in the engrailed domain of wing discs.
source: However, upon heat shock to induce FLP expression, robust cell death occurs in a mosaic pattern specifically in the engrailed domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary Figure 3-1C-D.

claim: Using DEMISE in the hindgut, low background level of cell death can be achieved followed by robust induction of cell death upon heat shock that occurs independently of transgene expression.
source: Again, using our most efficacious DEMISE/FLP combination in the hindgut, we can achieve a low background level of cell death (Figure 3C,D,F), followed by robust induction of cell death upon heat shock that occurs independently of transgene expression (Figure 3C–F, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Fizzy-related (Fzr) is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian FZR1/CDH1.
source: Fizzy-related (Fzr), the Drosophila homolog of mammalian FZR1/CDH1, is a binding partner of the APC/C, which facilitates degradation of mitotic cyclins including Cyclin B.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Fzr.

claim: Fzr is a binding partner of the APC/C, which facilitates degradation of mitotic cyclins including Cyclin B.
source: Fizzy-related (Fzr), the Drosophila homolog of mammalian FZR1/CDH1, is a binding partner of the APC/C, which facilitates degradation of mitotic cyclins including Cyclin B.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Fzr function.

claim: Fzr is a well-known regulator of the endocycle in many cell types.
source: Fzr is also a well-known regulator of the endocycle in many cell types (Lehner and O'Farrell, 1989; Schaeffer et al., 2004; Sigrist and Lehner, 1997; Stormo and Fox, 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: fzr mutant cells can ectopically undergo mitotic cycles instead of endocycles.
source: and fzr mutant cells can ectopically undergo mitotic cycles instead of endocycles (Schaeffer et al., 2004; Schoenfelder et al., 2014; Sigrist and Lehner, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Using two independent fzr enhancer traps, fzr expression is high in the adult pylorus, whereas fzr is undetectable in the larval pylorus.
source: Indeed, using two independent fzr enhancer traps, fzr expression is high in the adult pylorus, whereas fzr is undetectable in the larval pylorus (Figure 4A–B', Figure 4—figure supplement 1L–M').
evidence: Supported by enhancer trap expression data in Figure 4A-B' and supplementary figures.

claim: Without injury, fzr knockdown did not noticeably alter hindgut development with the exception of the rectal papillae.
source: Without injury, fzr knockdown did not noticeably alter hindgut development with the exception of the rectal papillae, where we previously identified a role for fzr in the pre-mitotic endocycles (Schoenfelder et al., 2014, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by observation and citation to previous work, with data in supplementary figures.

claim: Following apoptotic injury induction, both control and fzr RNAi-expressing animals contain both TUNEL positive nuclei and pycnotic nuclei.
source: Following apoptotic injury induction, both control and fzr RNAi-expressing animals contain both TUNEL positive nuclei and pycnotic nuclei (Figure 4D–F)
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Lack of fzr does not alter the number of adult pyloric cells entering the cell cycle as seen by BrdU staining.
source: Further, lack of fzr does not alter the number of adult pyloric cells entering the cell cycle as seen by BrdU staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by BrdU quantification in supplementary figure.

claim: Following 5 days of recovery from adult injury, the adult pylorus of fzr flies completely restores pre-injury cell number and ploidy.
source: Strikingly, following 5 days of recovery from adult injury, the adult pylorus of fzr flies completely restores pre-injury cell number and ploidy (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4G-J.

claim: During injury recovery, mitotic cells are visible in the adult fzr pylorus (5/7 animals), but not in control animals (0/17 animals).
source: Further, during injury recovery, mitotic cells are visible in the adult fzr pylorus (5/7 animals), but not in control animals (0/17 animals, as assayed by PH3 and the centrosomal marker Centrosomin- Cnn, Figure 4K–L''').
evidence: Supported by PH3 and Centrosomin staining data in Figure 4K-L'''.

claim: In control adults, pyloric cells undergoing injury-induced endocycles only exhibit early replication patterns as assayed by BrdU.
source: In control adults, pyloric cells undergoing injury-induced endocycles only exhibit early replication patterns (as assayed by BrdU, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the S-phase pattern of many endocycling cells that undergo under-replication.
evidence: Supported by BrdU staining pattern in supplementary figure.

claim: DNA FISH shows that a satellite DNA repeat that is commonly under-replicated in endocycling cells does not increase in intensity in proportion to the nuclear size increase induced by adult pyloric injury.
source: In agreement with this idea, DNA FISH shows that a satellite DNA repeat that is commonly under-replicated in endocycling cells (Endow and Gall, 1975) does not increase in intensity in proportion to the obvious nuclear size increase induced by adult pyloric injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–O).
evidence: Supported by DNA FISH data in supplementary figure.

claim: In fzr animals, both early and late-S patterns are exhibited after injury.
source: In contrast, fzr animals instead exhibit both early and late-S patterns after injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by BrdU staining pattern in supplementary figure.

claim: The two distinct injury-induced cell cycle programs in the pylorus are dictated by the action of Fzr, a conserved negative regulator of mitotic cyclins.
source: Taken together, we find the two distinct injury-induced cell cycle programs in the pylorus are dictated by the action of Fzr, a conserved negative regulator of mitotic cyclins (Figure 4M).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fzr knockdown experiments.

claim: Either with or without injury, adult pyloric cells do not express Hindsight.
source: Either with or without injury, adult pyloric cells do not express Hindsight, suggesting that this Notch target is not involved in the pyloric cell cycle injury response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by Hindsight staining data in supplementary figure.

claim: Expressing dominant negative Notch receptor throughout pupation using DEMISE does not prevent injury-mediated endocycles in the adult pylorus.
source: Further, expressing dominant negative Notch receptor throughout pupation using DEMISE does not prevent injury-mediated endocycles in the adult pylorus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I), despite the fact that we observe expected Notch phenotypes in the rectal papillae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–K, Fox et al., 2010; Schoenfelder et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary figures showing Notch manipulation effects.

claim: Unlike previous studies on developmental endocycles, the results suggest a Notch-independent, fzr-dependent alteration in injury cell cycle responses in the Drosophila pylorus.
source: Thus, unlike previous studies on developmental endocycles, our results suggest a Notch-independent, fzr-dependent alteration in injury cell cycle responses in the Drosophila pylorus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Notch and fzr manipulation experiments.

claim: Activation of the pro-growth signaling Ras pathway is linked to ploidy increases in cardiac tissue in flies and mammals.
source: Activation of the pro-growth signaling Ras pathway, which is well-known to drive cell number increases in many contexts, is also linked to ploidy increases in cardiac tissue in flies and mammals (Hunter et al., 1995; Wu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Larval RasV12 expression nearly triples the adult pyloric cell number without a substantial change in nuclear size.
source: Cell number counts and size measurements show that larval RasV12 expression nearly triples the adult pyloric cell number without a substantial change in nuclear size (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5G, H.

claim: Following RasV12 expression in the adult, the adult pylorus expands in size with no increase in cell number, while instead the nuclear size increases.
source: As with larval RasV12 expression, the adult pylorus expands in size following RasV12 expression (Figure 5C,E). However, and in parallel with our injury results, we observe no increase in cell number, while instead the nuclear size increases (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5G, H.

claim: These data are consistent with RasV12 inducing endocycles in the mature adult pylorus.
source: These data are consistent with RasV12 inducing endocycles in the mature adult pylorus.
evidence: Inference from RasV12 expression data showing increased nuclear size without cell number increase.

claim: fzr suppresses nuclear size expansion in RasV12 expressing adults.
source: As in our injury studies, fzr suppresses nuclear size expansion in RasV12 expressing adults (Figure 5C,F,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5C, F, H.

claim: The overall pyloric cell number increases ~20% above controls in fzr RNAi + RasV12 animals.
source: Further, the overall pyloric cell number increases ~20% above controls in fzr RNAi + RasVV12 animals, consistent with a role of fzr in preventing aberrant cellular hyperplasia in the adult pylorus (Figure 5C,E–G).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5C, E-G.

claim: The tissue expansion caused by RasV12 expression does not substantially distort the epithelial architecture.
source: The tissue expansion caused by RasV12 expression does not substantially distort this epithelial architecture (Figure 5J–J').
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 5J-J'.

claim: 23.3% (±3.3% SEM) of fzr RNAi +RasV12 animals examined show severe distortions of the intestinal epithelial architecture.
source: Specifically, 23.3% (±3.3% SEM) of fzr RNAi +RasVV12 animals examined show severe distortions of the intestinal epithelial architecture, either into or away from the intestinal lumen (Figure 5K–K', L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C''').
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5L and imaging data.

claim: Adult pyloric area actually decreases in fzr RNAi +RasV12 animals relative to animals expressing RasV12 alone.
source: These distortions were not caused by increased tissue area in fzr RNAi +RasVV12 animals, as adult pyloric area actually decreases in these animals relative to animals expressing RasV12 alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, see Discussion for proposed mechanism).
evidence: Supported by quantification in supplementary Figure 5-1D.

claim: Only fzr RNAi +RasV12 animals show substantial permeability of the epithelial barrier.
source: Using the well-established 'Smurf' assay (Rera et al., 2011; see Materials and methods) we observed that only fzr RNAi +RasVV12 animals show substantial permeability of the epithelial barrier.
evidence: Supported by Smurf assay data and citation to the assay method.

claim: The frequency of fzr RNAi +RasV12 animals with a permeable epithelial barrier (17.33% ± 3.18% SEM) is very similar to the proportion of animals of this same genotype with epithelial architecture distortions.
source: We note that the frequency of fzr RNAi +RasVV12 animals with a permeable epithelial barrier (17.33% ± 3.18% SEM, Figure 5M) is very similar to the proportion of animals of this same genotype with epithelial architecture distortions (Figure 5L vs. M), implying that these defects may be related.
evidence: Supported by comparison of quantifications in Figure 5L and 5M.

claim: Under conditions of prolonged growth signaling, endocycles protect the pyloric epithelium against hyperplasia, distortions in epithelial lumen architecture, and gut barrier permeability.
source: Thus, under conditions of prolonged growth signaling, endocycles protect the pyloric epithelium against hyperplasia, distortions in epithelial lumen architecture, and gut barrier permeability (Figure 5N).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RasV12 and fzr manipulation experiments.

claim: Ploidy increases in the repairing pylorus are perfectly tuned to replace the pre-injury number of genomes.
source: First, using the simplicity of our system, we discovered that ploidy increases in the repairing pylorus are perfectly tuned to replace the pre-injury number of genomes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genome content quantification data.

claim: Reverting adult endocycles to mitotic cycles in the injured adult also leads to the correct number of pre-injury cells with no ploidy increase.
source: Further, reverting adult endocycles to mitotic cycles in the injured adult also leads to the correct number of pre-injury cells with no ploidy increase, suggesting that both mitotic cycles and endocycles are able to accurately replace lost tissue mass/genome content.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fzr knockdown experiments in injured adults.

claim: Both mitotic cycles and endocycles are able to accurately replace lost tissue mass/genome content.
source: Further, reverting adult endocycles to mitotic cycles in the injured adult also leads to the correct number of pre-injury cells with no ploidy increase, suggesting that both mitotic cycles and endocycles are able to accurately replace lost tissue mass/genome content.
evidence: Inference from comparison of injury responses with and without fzr.

claim: Endocycles enable the pylorus to resist tissue malformation and permeability phenotypes under conditions of sustained tissue growth signaling.
source: Second, using a RasV12 model, we present evidence that endocycles enable the pylorus to resist tissue malformation and permeability phenotypes under conditions of sustained tissue growth signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RasV12 experiments comparing endocycles vs mitotic cycles.

claim: Endocycles are employed in some tissues to maintain epithelial integrity in the face of stresses such as injury or excess growth signaling.
source: As activated Ras/Raf signaling reproduces the injury responsive cell cycles in our system and in injured cardiac tissues, this model may suggest that endocycles are employed in some tissues to maintain epithelial integrity in the face of stresses such as injury or excess growth signaling.
evidence: Speculation based on findings in this study and comparison to cardiac tissues.

claim: The heart has one of the lowest incidences of cancers of any organ.
source: In line with this idea, we note that of any organ, the heart has one of the lowest incidences of cancers (Bisel et al., 1953; Leja et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A recent study showed a tumor-protective role of polyploidy in the liver.
source: and a recent study also showed a tumor-protective role of polyploidy in the liver (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: While both injury-induced and developmental endocycles rely on Fzr, the upstream regulation in the injury context does not involve regulation of Notch.
source: Our results show that, while both injury-induced and developmental endocycles rely on Fzr, the upstream regulation in the injury context does not involve regulation of Notch, a well-known developmental endoreplication regulator in flies and mammals (Cornejo et al., 2011; Deng et al., 2001; Domanitskaya and SchupbachSchüpbach, 2012; Mercher et al., 2008; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Poirault-Chassac et al., 2010; Shcherbata et al., 2004; Sun and Deng, 2007; Von Stetina et al., 2018).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Notch manipulation experiments and comparison to cited developmental studies.

claim: Loss of fzr alone is sufficient to restore pyloric mitosis.
source: It is somewhat surprising that loss of fzr alone is sufficient to restore pyloric mitosis, as the cyclin dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) activator Cdc25/String is often required (Schaeffer et al., 2004; Von Stetina et al., 2018).
evidence: Observation from fzr knockdown experiments with comparison to cited work.

claim: In the pylorus, Cdk1 may be primed for activity but is kept inactive without its cyclin binding partners, which are negatively regulated by high levels of APC/Fzr.
source: Thus, in the pylorus, Cdk1 may be primed for activity but is kept inactive without its cyclin binding partners, which are negatively regulated by high levels of APC/Fzr.
evidence: Speculation based on fzr knockdown results and known Cdk1 regulation.

claim: In the normally quiescent adult stage, induced cell proliferation may be more detrimental for tissue integrity than induced endocycles.
source: As our data suggest, in the normally quiescent adult stage, induced cell proliferation may be more detrimental for tissue integrity than induced endocycles.
evidence: Speculation based on RasV12 experiments showing tissue architecture defects with mitosis.

claim: Building new tissues during intestinal development necessitates the use of cell division.
source: However, building new tissues during intestinal development necessitates the use of cell division.
evidence: Logical inference about developmental requirements.

claim: The Dipteran intestine is completely remodeled during metamorphosis, and cell divisions from the pylorus are the source of the majority of new hindgut cells.
source: For poorly understood reasons, the Dipteran intestine is completely remodeled during metamorphosis, and cell divisions from the pylorus are the source of the majority of new hindgut cells (Aghajanian et al., 2016; Bodenstein, 1950; Fox and Spradling, 2009; Robertson, 1936; Sawyer et al., 2017; Takashima et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Once organ remodeling is complete, the pylorus, which lacks stem cells, then ceases to divide.
source: Once organ remodeling is complete, the pylorus, which lacks stem cells, then ceases to divide (Fox and Spradling, 2009; Sawyer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At the point when organ remodeling is complete, high fzr levels prevent any future cell division.
source: Our data suggest that at this point, high fzr levels prevent any future cell division.
evidence: Inference from fzr expression data and knockdown experiments.

claim: Following injury, there may be an increased negative regulation of mitotic entry, as polyploid cell division causes genomic instability.
source: Following injury, there may be an increased negative regulation of mitotic entry, as we and others have shown that polyploid cell division causes genomic instability (Davoli et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2010; Fox et al., 2010; Hassel et al., 2014; Schoenfelder et al., 2014; Storchová et al., 2006).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to previous work on polyploid cell division.

claim: DEMISE is amenable to injury studies in the imaginal disc.
source: We show that this system is amenable to injury studies in the imaginal disc, a widely used tissue injury system (Harris et al., 2016; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments in wing imaginal discs.

claim: Other tissues with injury responses that would benefit from DEMISE include the stem cell-based midgut, the brain, the abdomen, the muscle and ovarian follicle cells.
source: Other tissues with injury responses that we have not tested but that would benefit from DEMISE as a tool include the stem cell-based midgut (Apidianakis and Rahme, 2009; Buchon et al., 2009; Chatterjee and Ip, 2009; Jiang et al., 2009), the brain (Moreno et al., 2015), the abdomen (Losick et al., 2013; Losick et al., 2016), the muscle (Chaturvedi et al., 2017) and ovarian follicle cells (Tamori and Deng, 2013).
evidence: Speculation about potential applications with citations to relevant tissue systems.

claim: The inducible reaper transgene can be used in studies of apoptotic signaling, such as the regulation of 'undead' cells.
source: Beyond studies of tissue injury, our inducible reaper transgene can be used in studies of apoptotic signaling, such as the regulation of 'undead' cells which contain active caspase signaling but persist and influence the behavior of neighboring cells (Deveraux et al., 1998; Fan and Bergmann, 2014; Hay et al., 1994; Ryoo et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation about potential applications with citations to relevant studies.

claim: There are vastly more currently available Gal4 and partner UAS lines than for LexA or Q systems.
source: While many dual transgene systems in flies combine Gal4 with either LexA or Q systems (Kockel et al., 2016; Lai and Lee, 2006; Potter et al., 2010), there are vastly more currently available Gal4 and partner UAS lines than for these other systems, making our system more immediately employable for the most cell types/transgenes.
evidence: Statement about available genetic tools with citations to other systems.

claim: The use of a single Gal4 promoter for both injury and transgene activation provides tissue specificity and ensures both injury and transgenes are expressed in the same population of cells.
source: Additionally, the use of a single Gal4 promoter for both injury and transgene activation provides tissue specificity and ensures both injury and transgenes are expressed in the same population of cells.
evidence: Description of DEMISE design feature.

claim: DEMISE could be adapted for use in other organisms by adapting existing FLP and Cre-mediated injury and gene knockout models.
source: Beyond Drosophila, we note that our system could be adapted for use in other organisms, by adapting existing FLP and Cre-mediated injury and gene knockout models.
evidence: Speculation about potential adaptation to other organisms.
